cells.tense: Something arrives and you let it, without hurrying it into an explanation.
cells.ask: Today, when something lands, sit one unhurried minute before you name it or solve it. Let it show you its own shape.
cells.core:
Something comes toward you and you let it land. No hurry to name it, file it, or explain it away — you can feel it before you know what it is, and that already works. This is how feeling moves when nobody is rushing it.

The heaviness you carry hasn't shut you down. You're still soft enough to be moved, which is rarer than staying hard through it. It holds as long as you let things come on their own clock. Ask for less proof than usual. One minute of plain feeling, before the explaining starts, keeps you in contact with what's here.

cells.tense: You're reaching for a feeling that hasn't shown up, bracing for the weight you expect to land.
cells.ask: Pick one moment today and stay in it as it is, without rehearsing what it should feel like. The next thing can wait until it's here.
cells.core:
You're carrying the next thing before it's here — before anyone's asked, before you know if it's yours to hold. The heart's open ahead of schedule, braced for a weight that hasn't shown up. It looks like being prepared. It spends hold on loads that aren't on you yet.

Feeling ahead of time is real, and being open isn't the fault. But when it runs things, you're seldom in the room you're actually in; you're in the one you're getting ready for. The balance comes back by choosing what's here, deliberately, not by feeling less. Let one thing be as it is, without pre-feeling it. The rest you can set down until it is real.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying tomorrow before it's arrived.

cells.tense: The letting-in stopped at some point, and you're still standing at that door.
cells.ask: Sit down for five minutes today and write one thing you feel as it happens. Don't judge it or fix it. Just put it on the page.
cells.core:
When you can feel things as they come and still carry what's heavy, that's the settled version, and you've lived it. The feeling came in, the weight got held, and the two didn't cancel each other. That's how it works when both are running.

Lately the feeling side went quiet. A door closed somewhere and holding kept going fine without it, so nothing forced it back open. The softness is still there behind that door. Opening it doesn't settle the past or fix anything old. It lets what's in front of you be new — no rehearsal, no verdict. Try one thing today you haven't felt before. Something small. The door isn't locked.

cells.tense: You take things in and it shapes your day, and you talk about it as if it were nothing.
cells.ask: Tonight, take one thing you felt today and say plainly, out loud, 'I felt that.' One sentence. No defense of it.
cells.core:
You take things in and it works. You feel a room before anyone speaks, you know where the weight is sitting, and it quietly changes how you hold things. That's the settled version, and it's already yours. The reading of a room is accurate, it arrives fast, and you act on it well.

But when it comes up, you shrug it off. Maybe you say you don't know why you did it that way. That knowing is yours; it's been steering this the whole time. Naming it isn't making a fuss — it's signing what you've already been doing. One honest sentence today. 'I felt that.' The rest stays yours, no explanation owed.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person has been through a loss or that their past is why they hold back; Too Little may locate them at that door but must not say what happened there or who was behind it. A reader might say 'I'm not cold, I'm just tired' — so the cell should describe a bend in how the feeling arrives, not their character, and the ask (one unhurried minute, feelings logged as they come) still leaves something usable even if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you've learned to endure by feeling nothing' — it sounds wise and tells them what they already know in a way that closes the door.
